guardianfootball.description: Says social media claims are ‘nonsense’ and ‘idiocy’ Coach sees ‘no reason to pay attention to these people’ Jürgen Klopp has reacted with disgust to a social media debate questioning whether the Germany team he is in the process of forming are “white enough”. Klopp said he believed there was no point in giving room to “such people and their utterances”, dismissing them as “complete nonsense”. Asked to respond to the debate as to whether the national team were “not German enough” or “not white enough”, he said: “There is absolutely no reason to pay attention to these people. You won’t get my thoughts on this. I have little time in everyday life for idiocy – and even less on social media.…

On a late summer’s afternoon at Crawley’s training ground in Sussex, Kazim-Richards, alongside his assistant, Julian Gray, the pair arriving in April and managing to save the club from relegation to the National League on the final day, speaks of the challenges ahead and how the team’s league position tells only…

pitchfork.description: Expanding dub techno’s spare grid toward rave and industrial, the UK trio’s newly reissued 1999 compilation summons roiling synth, excoriating feedback, and percussion that feels almost improvisatory.

pitchfork.description: The Swedish pop singer’s sixth album mainly leans on a familiar, hedonistic electro-pop sound. Its best moments explore what happens when full-bodied pleasure meets a fearful mind.

pitchfork.title: Bubble Treasure

pitchfork.title: Popstar
pitchfork.description: Tinashe’s eighth album is her best and bravest yet: more ambitious, more focused, and effortlessly in touch with the zeitgeist. It’s the best pop album of the year.

pitchfork.title: Westside Whimsy
pitchfork.description: After records steeped in grief and heartbreak, the singer’s latest album is framed as a laid-back ode to Los Angeles, but it can be tough to tease out the substance behind the sunny vibes.

pitchfork.title: Intentions
pitchfork.description: On her International Anthem debut, the Los Angeles-based singer threads R&B, jazz, and downbeat electronic into lovestruck reveries that still feel true to life.

pitchfork.title: Dream House
pitchfork.description: Lorely Rodriguez’s fifth album contends with the grief of losing her childhood home in a wildfire. These songs still center her virtuosic voice, but sometimes smother her eccentric perspective.

quietus.title: Album of the Week: Vanishing Twin’s Archives
quietus.description: Absence makes the art grow bolder says Will Ainsley about Archives, which sounds like Chiastic Slide-era Autechre reimagining the Wicker Man soundtrack Archives by Vanishing Twin The idea that an album could be made piecemeal, in different countries, via the internet, would have been inconceivable forty years ago. Such technology would have seemed strange; stranger still might have been the idea that the traditional method – that is, recording a series of songs in one place during a set period of time – is far less viable these days. The logistical demands of creative practice in 2026 mean a piecemeal approach is an all-too necessary solution for many artists. Studios and practice spaces…

Other photographs: Yaz Saoudi Tears Of The Patriarch is Lias Saoudi's second book, due to be published by White Rabbit early next year. In 2014 Lias and his brother Yaz travelled to North Africa to recreate the 'Bittersweet Symphony' for an experimental Fat White Family single about circumcision. Which was all fun and games until the pair ended up in Algerian jail... All these bands speaking in regional accents instead of singing, it vexed me. Vexed me because I have no region. Vexed me because it seemed like a cult of…

quietus.title: Public Enemy’s Apocalypse 91 The Enemy Strikes Black Revisited 35 years on
quietus.description: Public Enemy's fourth album is often overlooked but it's a true killer, says Angus Batey When the greatness of Public Enemy is discussed – which is often, for the band were, and indeed still are, one of the most consistently inventive, provocative and excellent outfits of the recorded-music-as-business era – the focus inevitably falls on their second and third albums. It Takes a Nation of Millions To Hold Us Back routinely turns up near the top of the all-time lists assembled by people who care about ensuring their opinions are thought sage; Fear Of A Black Planet, its follow-up, is actually its better, though its sonics had been well enough trailed and it perhaps therefore lacked the…

quietus.title: Curbside Lambsear – Put Rings On All My Fingers To Weigh Down My Hands
quietus.description: Curbside Lambsear Put Rings On All My Fingers To Weigh Down My Hands Members of The Umlauts and caroline find scrappy joy in dissonant chaos mixed with cinematic grandeur Put Rings On All My Fingers To Weigh Down My Hands by Curbside Lambsear This is an intriguingly hard-to-pin-down debut from London’s Curbside Lambsear, AKA Magdalena McLean and Annabelle Mödlinger. Having met while playing in the (still active) art punk band The Umlauts, the duo assembled this lengthy EP in a patchwork fashion. You wouldn't know it. There’s a coherent sense of purpose to these five tracks, as well as a free-roaming attitude when it comes to genre.

It features highlights and rarities from across the band's discography, including a special new re-working of 'New Paths To Helicon 1', featuring the Budapest Art Orchestra and orchestrated by Stars Of The Lid's Adam Wiltzie. Lucy Railton provides cello accompaniment on Burning Song,…

quietus.description: It's the artist's first album in over a decade David Sylvian has shared details of a new album, The Distance Between The Killer And The Killing. Comprised of recording sessions dating from 2012 to 2025, it marks the artist's first album in over a decade. The LP is based on recomposed improvisational sessions with musicians such as Ryuichi Sakamoto, Otomo Yoshihide, Bilianna Voutchkova, Miako Klein and more. The record is entirely instrumental, and is made up of one 46-minute piece. It follows 2009 album Manafon. NANOQ will release The Distance Between The Killer And The Killing on 26 February 2027. ...

Howley provides vocals for four tracks on Late Loop, while longtime collaborator Alison Skidmore contributes vocals to the other four songs on the album. Stott gave himself a number of parameters when he set out working on the record, deciding to use no basslines, no reverb and no effects, save for a delay unit. aquariumdrunkard.title: Dur-Dur Band :: Volume 3 (1988) & Volume 4 (1989)
aquariumdrunkard.description: The latest archival installment from the Somalian hotel band shows an unwieldy group streamlining their sound in the studio, dialing up the hooks, battening down the rhythms and keeping the grooves on point. Taking inspiration from Motown and disco as much as reggae and Afrobeat, the Dur-Dur Band kept the wild 70s alive even as the ugly 80s were taking over.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Transmissions :: Johnny Marr
aquariumdrunkard.description: Certain people play guitar in a way that is immediately recognizable, no matter the context. Our guest this week on Transmissions, Johnny Marr, is one such guitarists. A founding member of legendary indie band The Smiths, his sound is undeniable a blend of jangle, chime, bite, and attitude. He's back with a new album The Age Of Everything, which he joins us to discuss. Along the way, we also get into the global influence of The Smiths, discuss how Black American musicians inspired his sound, and share some of his less apparent influences, including Neil Young, who if you hear Marr tell it, played a rather pivotal role in the development of British punk rock. Style, sound, and the…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Future Sounds Of Jazz Vol. 16
aquariumdrunkard.description: Future Sounds of Jazz Vol. 16 is both a forecast and a wormhole. Across two discs, Michael Reinboth and Michael Rütten move through jazz, dub, electronic music, improvisation, and psychedelia with the intuitive logic of a late-night DJ set. The result is a strange, elastic universe of DJ Oil, Bitchin Bajas, Booker Stardrum, Nico Zam, Ilhan Ersahin, and Momoko Gill—and a reminder that the future of jazz remains gloriously undefined.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Protomartyr :: Hotel Usona
aquariumdrunkard.description: Protomartyr’s seventh album Hotel Usona (short for United States of North America) creates a fitting soundtrack as the country is pummeled by bad reviews. The Detroit veteran band envisions their homeland as a decrepit hotel where one of the TV channels is a live feed from Trump-Kennedy Center. The hotel is coincidentally located in Anacita, a fictional coastal town created by Casey for 2017’s Relatives in Descent. It’s the kind of place where the “liberal-minded close their eyes and dream of technology and kombucha.”

aquariumdrunkard.title: Lee Ranaldo :: Guitar-Centric Film Soundtracks
aquariumdrunkard.description: As a member of Sonic Youth, Drift, and his many other musical detours, Lee Ranaldo has treated the guitar as a pure sound source, creating dynamic new expressions in rock & roll and the avant-garde alike. But Ranaldo's new project, a soundtrack to director Joris Postema’s "eco-doc" The System, presents a new side of Lee, that of a filmic composer. To commemorate the album's release, Ranaldo sent over notes about nine other guitar-centric soundtracks that serve as conceptual inspirations for The System.

aquariumdrunkard.title: The Aquarium Drunkard Guide to Across the Horizon
aquariumdrunkard.description: What, exactly, is Across the Horizon? It could be accurately described as a podcast, a radio show, an imprint or even a genre; it’s also resulted in a host of compelling collaborations and a series of songs that push at the boundaries of what could be considered ambient music. "It’s like watching a musical community grow in real time," says Bob Holmes. Here’s a look at 10 standout songs from Across the Horizon thus far — music that demonstrates the breadth of the series as a whole.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Dungen :: Vidrig Vår
aquariumdrunkard.description: On the veteran Swedish outfit's most pared down and elegant affair, Vidrig Vår showcases Dungen still operating on a psychedelic wavelength not found elsewhere. Built around bandleader Gustav Ejste's panoramic piano progressions, the ballad-centric record flows with the weightless springtime atmosphere of the band's organically cinematic orbit.

mubi.description: From left to right: Cinematographer Peter Zeitlinger, director Werner Herzog, and stars Rooney Mara and Kate Mara shooting Bucking Fastard (2026). Courtesy of Gateway to Orkney LLC. Werner Herzog’s first fiction film in seven years, Bucking Fastard (2026),stands as one of his most bizarre. That’s high praise for a director who’s pulled 300-plus-ton steamships over mountains ( Fitzcarraldo , 1982), hypnotized his actors ( Heart of Glass , 1976), and followed “deranged” penguins across Antarctica ( Encounters at the End of the World , 2007). Herzog’s entire oeuvre teems with drifters pursuing quixotic dreams, people and stories often so odd as to strain credulity. But rarely has that…

In 2005, during a television interview in Italy, Giuseppe “Pino” Pelosi—AKA “The Frog”—recanted his confession about murdering Pier Paolo Pasolini on a beach in Ostia 30 years earlier. He claimed that it had been extracted by coercion and threats of violence, against both himself and his family (Pelosi was seventeen at the time). He also said that the legendary director’s death was a political killing disguised as a crime of passion—the premeditated and methodical muzzling of a “Dirty Communist.” Sergio Citti, a close friend of Pasolini, contributed to the controversy by suggesting that the filmmaker had been lured to the water…

mubi.description: Life of Jorge Luis Borges (Mariano Llinás, 2026). Words mean things, but that meaning is always changing. Sometimes those changes are organic, a gradual movement that is driven by the changing needs of speakers. But sometimes those changes are engineered from above, to serve the needs of those in power. nautilus.description: There have been many milestones of note in the story of the Space Age, but the launch of the USSR’s Sputnik 1 satellite is the major breakthrough that started it all. It was the first human-made object to get up into space and stay in orbit, having blasted off on October 4, 1957, from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in current-day Kazakhstan. It was a technological leap that no one outside the Soviet Union expected, including the U.S. The rush of rapid political, military, and scientific developments that followed—up to and beyond the 1969 moon landing—can all be traced back to this 23-inch-diameter metal sphere.
